Design and Construction of Lepidopteran, an
Electric Unmanned Hydrofoil Vessel
Robert Saylor1 and Lauren Zitzman2
Florida Keys – Unmanned Category
1 College of the Florida Keys
2 University of FloridaLepidopteran 2

or supercavitating. The Shutt strut also has the advantage of only using a single pivot point as the height
finding mechanism, eliminating complicated electronic or hydraulic pitch control systems.
The statement of requirements for the Lepidopteran is as follows: Total cost must be no more than $5500;
the vessel should be easily handled by two people, and preferably car-toppable; cruise speed should be 15
m/s (30 kn) and 20 m/s (40 kn) should be achievable for short bursts; and total battery capacity must be
enough to complete the 2 mile course with a 100% reserve.
Therefore, the general design chosen was to be an all-moving hydrofoil of the conventional airplane
configuration, as this layout is most efficient (TR 463-1). The hydrofoils would be solid, instead of flapped,
so that they could be upgraded to a supercavitating design in the future. We stuck with a more conservative
subcavitating design for our submission to avoid taking on too many risky points of failure for a new team. In
general, our philosophy has been to find inexpensive simple solutions where available (such as the
windsurfer hull) to focus our efforts on specific systems with the most potential reward, like the foils and
propeller.
DESIGN
Hull
Desirable characteristics of the hull include: light weight; high stability; and low drag. A used windsurf board
meets all of these requirements, while being inexpensive. The 2007 TIGA HyperX acquired for the project
weighs 8kg, has a length of 242 cm, and beam of 81 cm. The hull volume of 130 L is enough to support the
weight of a person sailing the board. This weight, 85 kg (~850 N), provides an approximate upper bound of
an acceptable all-up weight. The board’s flat bottom promotes early planing, and the low profile reduces
aerodynamic drag.
A custom-built hull was considered, but the cost was prohibitive for only marginal gains over the $50 Tiga.
Conservatively, a proposed 8ft scow hull would require at least $430 in materials (foam $90, carbon fiber
$240, resin $100) and 40 man-hours.
Weight and Balance
Table 1 shows the weights of the major components. The vessel was
floated and loaded with weights to produce a slightly bow-up pitch at
rest. The center of gravity was then measured, and the components
placed to maintain that CoG. The payload can then be shifted fore-andaft during testing for optimum performance underway.
Battery
Due to the weight sensitivity of foiling vessels, cell weight was the primary consideration. This immediately
eliminated lead-acid chemistry and put lithium-iron-phosphate at a disadvantage. Despite their good
performance, most prismatic cells were also eliminated by high weight and cost when configured in series.
Continuous current rating needed to be higher than the cruise motor current, and preferably higher than the
maximum motor current. The total energy stored had to be enough to complete the course with a 100%
reserve capacity. At a cruise speed of 15 m/s and current draw of 100 A at a nominal voltage of 48V, the 2-
mile course would be completed in 0.06 h, resulting in a power expenditure of 286 Wh.

While the capacity of the Panasonic 14s with respect to weight and cost is only middling, in absolute terms
it has the lightest weight while still meeting the current requirements and an acceptable reserve capacity.
The Samsung INR was a close second, but it would’ve needed to be doubled in parallel to meet the reserve
capacity requirements. It still would’ve been very competitive in terms of both absolute cost and weight, but
ultimately the Panasonic 14s was chosen to avoid the complication of extra wiring and because the
prismatic cells would be easier to cool.
Due to concerns about keeping the electronics watertight in case of a capsize, the battery does not have air
cooling. If testing shows that battery temperatures are unacceptable, a water-cooling plate will be added.
Foils
Section
Foil section choice drives the lift, drag, pitching moment, cavitation, and structural characteristics of the 3-
dimensional hydrofoil. Lifting foils need to produce lift equal to the weight of the vessel, while vertical struts
need to support the lifting foils and resist side loads induced by turns. Xflr5 was used to produce lift and drag
estimates, as well as pressure distributions that were then plotted in gnuplot to produce the cavitation
diagrams. Re = 1.38 million.
Table 3: Lifting Section Comparison
Thickness (%) At (%) Camber (%) At (%)
Eppler 817 10.98 32.83 2.88 68.87
Speer H105 12.55 39.54 1.69 65.17
NACA 63-412 12.00 34.93 2.20 50.05
Table 3 shows the summary information for the three lifting foils considered. Lepidopteran 5

Table 4 shows the second moment of inertia for each section, in terms of a percentage compared to a
rectangular section length 1 and thickness 0.12. A higher value is advantageous as stiffer sections can
achieve higher aspect ratios and therefore higher lift to drag ratios. The moment is influenced by the section
thickness, camber, and distribution of area.
Cavitation is caused by local pressure dropping below the vapor pressure of
water. The water boils, reducing lift and causing erosion of the hydrofoil
surface. This can occur on the upper surface at approximately the maximum
thickness (caused by high speeds), on the top of the leading edge (caused by
high AoA) or below the leading edge (caused by low AoA). Figure 1 is the
cavitation diagram for the three selected lifting foils. The dashed lines
represent freestream velocity (vessel speed) while the dotted lines represent
foil loading. If the foil loading intercepts the left side of the cavitation curve,
this represents cavitation on the bottom of the leading edge; if the foil loading
intercepts the right side of the curve, this represents upper leading-edge
cavitation; and if the foil loading intercepts the bottom of the curve this
represents high speed upper surface cavitation. The region inside the bucket
is cavitation-free operation. It is immediately apparent that the Speer H105
offers superior performance in every practical operating regime.
Figure 1: Lifting Section Cavitation Comparison

symmetrical sections are different since they spend the majority of the time producing no (or relatively small

and the criteria will instead depend on the lift and drag performance, and structural and ease of construction
concerns. The NACA 16-012 and NACA 66-012 had slightly deeper but very narrow drag buckets, and were
eliminated because of the difficulty of keeping them operating in such a narrow range of lift coefficients. The
NACA 64-012, 64-012A, and 65-012 had practically indistinguishable lift to drag curves. Therefore, the 64-
012A was selected for the aft foil because of the marginally higher sectional modulus and the thicker tail
being easier to manufacture.
The section NACA 16-012 was selected for the forward foil struts. Because turns make up only a very small
portion of the race, the struts operate close to zero AoA almost all of the time, and a lower minimum drag is
a beneficial trade-off. The considerably higher sectional modulus also means the strut can be made thinner
for the same structural requirements, reducing drag.
Figure 2: symmetrical Sections Cavitation Diagram
Area and Span
Forward
Foil area is driven by the amount of lift required (and therefore weight of the vessel) and desired take-off
speed. The forward foil bears 80% of the vessel weight, and is sized to operate at 15 m/s at a Cl of 0.5 (Cl/Cd Lepidopteran 7

= 62) . This results in a combined planform area of 116 cm2. Cl/Cd at 20 m/s is 46 (Cl = 0.28) and take-off
occurs at 9.7 m/s at a Cl/Cd of 69 (Cl = 1.2). Peak Cl/Cd is 76 at Cl = 0.95, corresponding to 10.9 m/s.
For each forward foil considered separately, a span of 24 cm and area of 58 cm2results in an aspect ratio of
9.9. Because the previous planform area calculations assume an infinite wing, this area must be adjusted
for finite wingspans. Also, the upper surface of the foil at the struct junction has reduced lift generation. The
area is therefore increased to make up for these losses (Vellinga, 2009) to 80.6 cm2 and the span to 27 cm.
Aft
The main role of the aft foil is pitch stability, and it is sized to operate at a wing loading one half of the forward
foil. This reduced wing loading causes automatic pitch stability, as any pitching of the vessel would cause
relatively larger changes of Cl and therefore lift on the more lightly loaded aft foil. (Vellinga, 2009). That area
of 58 cm2results in a Cl/Cd of 30 (Cl = 0.25) at 15 m/s and a Cl/Cd of 22 (Cl = 0.14) at 20 m/s. Take-off speed
would be 6.85 m/s at a Cl/Cd of 68 (Cl = 1.2). Because this speed is lower than the take-off speed of the main
foil, the vessel would have sufficient pitch authority to avoid squatting during take-off.
The same aspect ratio adjustments were made to the aft foil. Because of the difficulty of constructing long
molds, both foils were considered to be span-limited and were given an elliptical planform with no washout
(Speer, n.d.).
A SolidWorks Simulation (Figure 3) was performed to estimate the maximum stress imparted on the foil. At
a steady state load of 167.2 N, the maximum stress on the part was 1.476 x 108 compared to a maximum
allowable stress of 8 x 108for carbon fiber reinforced plastic (Vellinga, 2009), resulting in a factor of safety
of 5.4.
Figure 3: Aft Foil Stress FEA
Drive System
Jet pumps have been used many times in hydrofoil applications, most notably the Boeing 929 Jetfoil, PGH2, and Pegasus class (Williams, 1983). However, a jet pump small enough to fit the Lepidopteran would be
very difficult to source and would require a water pickup to be integrated into hydrofoil. A straight shaft Lepidopteran 8

inboard system would reduce transmission losses but would require a very long strut and accompanying
high drag loses while still producing a poor thrust angle. Therefore, an off-the-shelf gasoline outboard was
selected. The midsection and lower unit were mated to the electric motor, while the cowling, powerhead,
and controls were discarded. The driveshaft-mounted impeller was removed to reduce drag. Instead,
coolant water will be picked up from the same inlet and circulated by a 12v pump.
Transmission
The lower unit has a ratio of 2.42 to 1 and a maximum input speed of 6000 RPM, resulting in an output speed
of 2600 RPM. Because it is difficult to find the exact motor that has peak power at 6000 RPM, the motor was
mated to the driveshaft with a Gates HTD timing belt. This gives more flexibility with motor selection and
allows changes in RPM and torque during testing. Although the factory input speed limit is 6000 RPM, this is
only limited by bearing rating. If torque is kept below the gearset limits, the input shaft speed could
potentially be expanded past the factory limit with pulley ratio changes.
Motor
The motor was sized based on the power demands required by the propeller, and the rated power of the
donor outboard (10 hp, 7.4 kW). Two motors were considered: the 5 kW BLDC from GoldenMotor, and the
BadAss 6245-155Kv from Innov8tive Designs. While the 6245 had a rated continuous output of 4.7 kW and
more favorable motor velocity constant, we decided against it due to concerns about exceeding the duty
cycle of such a lightly constructed motor, as well as the difficulty of cooling and mounting an outrunner. A
number of no-name BLDC motors are available from outlets such as Amazon or Flipsky, but these products
were not even considered due to a lack of quality control and documentation.
Propeller
The factory propeller has three blades and measures 9.5 inches (24 cm) in diameter and 10 inches (25.4 cm)
in pitch. Assuming a slip of 5% and input shaft speed of 6000 RPM, this gives a maximum boat speed of only
9.4 m/s (18.2 kn). Aftermarket propellers are available with up to 12 inches of pitch. With the same
parameters, the maximum boat speed would be 11.8 m/s (23.0 kn). To meet the speed goal of 20 m/s, either
the existing propeller options must be spun twice as fast, or a higher pitch propeller must be designed. The
most common series, the Wageningen B-series, only covers P/D ratios up to 1.4. Other series, such as the
Gawn, KCA, and Newton-Rader, cover P/D ratios up to 2. The Newton-Rader series was selected because
they published both cavitation data and tabulated figures that were easier to work with. However, the Gawn
and KCA series offered similar performance. While a propeller with a diameter of 24 cm and a pitch of 50 cm
would reach the 20 m/s goal at a propeller shaft speed of 2500 RPM, it would do so with a power requirement
of over 20 kW. Thus, a compromise approach is necessary: The gearbox will run at a 50% overspeed to turn
a propeller 16 cm in diameter and 33.3 cm in pitch. At a full propeller RPM of 3750, the propeller will produce
341 N of thrust at an input power of 7.85 kW. This excess above the 5 kW motor rating is acceptable for short
duty cycle sprint speed goal of 20 kn. At a cruise speed of 15 m/s and propeller RPM of 3000, the propeller
will produce 286 N of thrust at an input power of 4.8 kW.
The Newton-Rader series assumes a hub to diameter ratio of 16.7%, while our lower unit geometry fixes hub
diameter at 6.6 cm. In lieu of a more advanced treatment, it was assumed that the thrust produced and
torque required would be reduced in proportion to the reduction in propulsor disk area. This 15% reduction
has already been accounted for in the calculations and figures. Wake fraction and thrust deduction were
both assumed to be zero, due to the high speed of the vessel and minimal hull interference. Lepidopteran 9

Figure 4 shows the amount of thrust produced as a function of vessel speed and propeller RPM, and figure
5 shows the same with the power required. The J values of 1.5 and 2.05 represent the lower and upper bound
of the 70% η efficiency band, while the 1.8 advance line is the peak operating point of 78% η efficiency.
Figure 4: Thrust Produced as a Function of Speed and RPM

Figure 6: Vessel Thrust and Drag as a Function of Speed
Figure 6 superimposes the thrust produced by the Newton-Rader 16 x 33.3 at different thrusts with the
estimated drag from the foils, struts, and gear case. This was done using the drag equation with Cd values
generated by xflr5. Notably, this does not include aerodynamic or hull drag, and the gearcase portion of the
drag is probably not very accurate, due to the irregular shape of the housing and ventilation fences.
Resistance towing tests were planned, but bad weather prevented any actual data collection, even though
this would’ve provided very accurate results. However, this figure does indicate that the speed goals are
feasible.
CONSTRUCTION
Power Storage and Transmission
A Husky storage container is used as a waterproof container for the electronics. The battery and other
components are bolted to the box which is then bolted to the deck. The battery negative terminal is wired to
a Jiabaida JBD-AP21S002 battery management system. This BMS monitors cell voltage imbalances, state of
charge, charge and discharge current, and battery temperature. It automatically isolates the battery if
voltage is ever too high or too low and features a customizable software fuse, set to 200 A. The positive Lepidopteran 11

terminal of the battery has a 400 A fusible link connected to a 400A contactor energized by a disconnect
button accessible on top of the vessel. The 4 AWG wire used is rated for 160 A continuous duty3, well in
excess of the 150 A intermittent and 100 A continuous motor demands. The speed controller is a Golden
Motor EZkontrol B48800, rated for a working voltage of 48 V (max 75V) and bus current of 400 A.
Figure 7: Electronics Compartment View with Labels
A 52V 14S Intelligent Lithium Smart Charger from HPCBikes provides a slow but reliable and inexpensive
charging current of 3 A.
Gearcase and Mounting
A sheet of G10 FRP was laminated to the top aft surface of the board with 8 layers of 4oz unidirectional
carbon fiber. A custom pivot tube was fabricated from aluminum plate and tube to replace the bulky and
heavy factory outboard mounting system. The tiller arm was cut off, and the assembly bolted to the mounting
plate. The lower unit was disassembled, the gear surfaces and bearings were inspected for wear, and
reassembled. The motor mounting plate was fabricated out of ¼” aluminum plate, and a bearing pressed
into the plate to support the driveshaft.
A Gates HTD 5mm pitch timing belt with a 15mm width was selected. The 25mm width would’ve allowed
more margin of safety on the allowable torque transmitted, but the 25mm width had a much worse selection
of pulleys. Instead of aluminum, they were cast steel, and there were fewer different teeth counts available.
The two ratios selected were 1.94:1 and 3:1, which roughly corresponds4 with spinning the driveshaft at 6000
and 9000 RPM from a loaded motor RPM of 2900. Also, intermediate ratios of 2.25:1 and 2.58:1 could be
achieved by mixing pulleys between the two sets, in case optimum performance is somewhere in between.
Belt tension is achieved by rotating the motor in the housing, much like an automotive v-belt. Unfortunately,
3 United States Coast Guard Electrical System Compliance Guideline
4 The exact ratios desired could not be sourced because not every tooth number pulley is manufactured, we had to
round to the closest ones available.Lepidopteran 12

as of the writing for this report, we are still waiting for the pulleys to be bored to fit the respective shafts
before being able to do on-the-water testing.
Figure 8: Gearbox, Motor, Mount, and Steering System
The Newton-Rader 16x33 propeller was modelled in SolidWorks to mate with a SOLAS RBX-A20 hub. The file
was then sent to the casting house to be 3D printed and investment cast in stainless steel.
Controls
Steering is controlled with a Savox SB-2290SG servo. It is rated for 70.0 kg-cm of
torque at 8.4 V. A bracket was fabricated and bolted to the outboard midsection
and a linkage connects to the servo arm.
The radio transmitter is a RadioMaster MT12 and the receiver is a RadioMaster
ER5C-i. They use the ELRS 2.4 GHz protocol, which offers superior flexibility for
programming and telemetry. A Speedybee F405 flight controller provides an
interface for telemetry data and (so far unutilized) autopilot functions. A Foxtech
HV BEC converts the main battery voltage to 8.4 V for the RC electronics and 12
V for the coolant pump.
The BLDC controller cannot interface directly with any of the RC electronics. The radio receiver outputs a 1
to 2 millisecond PWM signal, while the controller expects a 0-5v analog
input. Instead, the receiver drives a throttle servo which mechanically
actuates a potentiometer to provide the necessary analog signal.
Foils
The foils are being constructed by vacuum bagged wet layup inside a
female half mold. The layup consists of 2 layers of 9 oz biaxial (±45 to the
Figure 9: N-R 16 x 33
Rendering
Figure 10: Aft Foil Mold RenderingLepidopteran 13

span axis) on the outside skin and the remaining interior of unidirectional fabric oriented along the span axis.
The parts will then be demolded, flattened along the neutral plane, and then bonded together. The struts will
then be bonded to the lifting foils, while the aft foil will be bolted directly to the lower unit cavitation plate.
The female molds have been 3d printed, and construction is currently ongoing.
TESTING AND EVALUATION
Due to many delays in fund processing, material delivery, and part fabrication, no on-the-water testing has
yet been done. However, everything is in order to perform testing and tuning over the next three weeks
leading into the competition. The questions that need to be answered are:
1. Which pulley ratios provide the best performance?
2. Which propeller provides the best performance?
3. What is the optimal CoG position?
4. Are motor, battery, and ESC cooling sufficient?
5. Is steering authority sufficient?
We can evaluate these conditions by running the vessel while changing one variable at a time. We can
directly monitor GPS speed, RPM, and component temperatures. By calculating slip from RPM and speed,
we can also find if the propeller is actually operating in an efficient regime. If battery cooling is insufficient,
a coolant plate can be added, and if the ESC and motor cooling is insufficient, the water pump could be
upgraded to a higher flow rate.
RISKS
There are three main weaknesses in our design:
1. The steering servo may have insufficient range or torque. The trade-off between torque and steering
range can be modified by lengthening or shortening the moment arm of either bracket. However,
while under load there will be much more force on the steering system than at rest, and it may prove
to be too much for the Savox servo. In that case, the servo can be replaced by a geared DC motor
with a reversible speed control that can output the torque required. However, since the race format
does not prioritize turning ability, it may be acceptable to just slow down for each turn.
2. Center of gravity may be too far aft. This can be determined by checking performance after relocating
the payload weight. If this is the case, the battery box could be moved further forward, which would
require new power cables; or the weight of the motor mounting plates and the outboard midsection
could be reduced by drilling lightening holes. Also, if there is extra buoyancy in the forward areas of
the hull, extra ballast could just be carried at the bow, or even extended in front of the bow on a sprit
structure. In the future, this imbalance could be mitigated by moving the motor forward of the pivot
point, but we chose the current location to simplify fabrication of the mounting plate and fitting of
the drive belt.
3. The gearbox may not be able to handle an input speed of 9000 RPM. We could not find any literature
discussing exactly why almost all outboard engines are limited to 6000 RPM, but hypothesize that is
only because of limitation in the combustion powerhead. The gear sets are typically limited by
torque, not RPM, and bearings of the size used in the lower unit usually have speed limits well over
10,000 RPM. Since this 50% was the only practical way to hit our speed targets, we considered this
an acceptable risk, especially considering the short duration of the race. By intentionally running the
lower unit under more demanding conditions during testing than during the race, by performing Lepidopteran 14

frequent oil changes, and by examining the gears and bearings for abnormal wear, we will find out if
running at the elevated speed is acceptable. If not, we will simply run the race at reduced speed.
FUTURE DEVELOPMENT
Lepidopteran is ripe for ongoing modification and use. The manageable size, high speed, good endurance,
and payload capacity mean it could be used for other marine projects as well as future PEP competitions.
The following are some of the avenues that we think may be worth pursuing:
1. Hydrofoils
a. The foil section, planform, or lift distribution could be improved. Particularly of interest may
be changing the elliptical planform to a bell-shaped lift distribution, which would be more
efficient with respect to strength.
b. The foil manufacturing process could be improved. Perhaps they could be milled out of billet
stainless steel (some of the latest Moth hydrofoils have done this), or just laid up with an
improved method, like VARTM.
c. The subcavitating foils could be changed to supercavitating. They would be more inefficient
but offer the possibility to break the 50 kn barrier.
d. The entire foil system could be switched to a surface piercing configuration.
2. Gearbox – the current lower unit gearbox is probably the single biggest area for improvement. The
outboard that we chose uses a through hub exhaust, which is bulky and increases drag of the lower
unit, while providing zero utility to an electric system. Also, the very low gear ratio of 2.42 to 1 is more
suited for a sailboat or a dinghy than a performance high speed vessel. Both of these aspects could
be improved by selecting a lower unit similar to those used by racing boats.

Electric Unmanned Hydrofoil Vessel
Robert Saylor1 and Lauren Zitzman2
Florida Keys – Unmanned Category
1 College of the Florida Keys
2 University of FloridaLepidopteran 2
TABLE OF CONTENTS
INTRODUCTION
Hydrofoils provide two main advantages to a vessel. First, the reduced wetted area decreases drag and
increases maximum speed. At 50 kn, the lift to drag ratio of a hydrofoil design is about twice that of a
conventional planing design (Clement, 1964). Second, by elevating the hull above the crest of waves,
maximum speed is effectively decoupled from sea state. Since electric vessels have lower energy storage
density than combustion fuels, maximizing efficiency is important to achieve usable ranges.
Submerged foils are usually more efficient than surface piercing designs because they tend to have higher
aspect ratios; and operate below the surface, instead of at the surface, which reduces ventilation. While
flapped foils can operate at larger ranges of lift coefficients, they tend to be higher drag and weaker because
of the hinge assembly. An all-moving design, like the Shutt strut (Vellinga, 2009) can be either subcavitating Lepidopteran 3
or supercavitating. The Shutt strut also has the advantage of only using a single pivot point as the height
finding mechanism, eliminating complicated electronic or hydraulic pitch control systems.
The statement of requirements for the Lepidopteran is as follows: Total cost must be no more than $5500;
the vessel should be easily handled by two people, and preferably car-toppable; cruise speed should be 15
m/s (30 kn) and 20 m/s (40 kn) should be achievable for short bursts; and total battery capacity must be
enough to complete the 2 mile course with a 100% reserve.
Therefore, the general design chosen was to be an all-moving hydrofoil of the conventional airplane
configuration, as this layout is most efficient (TR 463-1). The hydrofoils would be solid, instead of flapped,
so that they could be upgraded to a supercavitating design in the future. We stuck with a more conservative
subcavitating design for our submission to avoid taking on too many risky points of failure for a new team. In
general, our philosophy has been to find inexpensive simple solutions where available (such as the
windsurfer hull) to focus our efforts on specific systems with the most potential reward, like the foils and
propeller.
DESIGN
Hull
Desirable characteristics of the hull include: light weight; high stability; and low drag. A used windsurf board
meets all of these requirements, while being inexpensive. The 2007 TIGA HyperX acquired for the project
weighs 8kg, has a length of 242 cm, and beam of 81 cm. The hull volume of 130 L is enough to support the
weight of a person sailing the board. This weight, 85 kg (~850 N), provides an approximate upper bound of
an acceptable all-up weight. The board’s flat bottom promotes early planing, and the low profile reduces
aerodynamic drag.
A custom-built hull was considered, but the cost was prohibitive for only marginal gains over the $50 Tiga.
Conservatively, a proposed 8ft scow hull would require at least $430 in materials (foam $90, carbon fiber
$240, resin $100) and 40 man-hours.

Battery
Due to the weight sensitivity of foiling vessels, cell weight was the primary consideration. This immediately
eliminated lead-acid chemistry and put lithium-iron-phosphate at a disadvantage. Despite their good
performance, most prismatic cells were also eliminated by high weight and cost when configured in series.
Continuous current rating needed to be higher than the cruise motor current, and preferably higher than the
maximum motor current. The total energy stored had to be enough to complete the course with a 100%
reserve capacity. At a cruise speed of 15 m/s and current draw of 100 A at a nominal voltage of 48V, the 2-
mile course would be completed in 0.06 h, resulting in a power expenditure of 286 Wh.

Section
Foil section choice drives the lift, drag, pitching moment, cavitation, and structural characteristics of the 3-
dimensional hydrofoil. Lifting foils need to produce lift equal to the weight of the vessel, while vertical struts
need to support the lifting foils and resist side loads induced by turns. Xflr5 was used to produce lift and drag
estimates, as well as pressure distributions that were then plotted in gnuplot to produce the cavitation
diagrams. Re = 1.38 million.

Cavitation is caused by local pressure dropping below the vapor pressure of
water. The water boils, reducing lift and causing erosion of the hydrofoil
surface. This can occur on the upper surface at approximately the maximum
thickness (caused by high speeds), on the top of the leading edge (caused by

this represents cavitation on the bottom of the leading edge; if the foil loading
intercepts the right side of the curve, this represents upper leading-edge
cavitation; and if the foil loading intercepts the bottom of the curve this
represents high speed upper surface cavitation. The region inside the bucket
is cavitation-free operation. It is immediately apparent that the Speer H105
offers superior performance in every practical operating regime.

Area and Span
Forward
Foil area is driven by the amount of lift required (and therefore weight of the vessel) and desired take-off
speed. The forward foil bears 80% of the vessel weight, and is sized to operate at 15 m/s at a Cl of 0.5 (Cl/Cd Lepidopteran 7
= 62) . This results in a combined planform area of 116 cm2. Cl/Cd at 20 m/s is 46 (Cl = 0.28) and take-off
occurs at 9.7 m/s at a Cl/Cd of 69 (Cl = 1.2). Peak Cl/Cd is 76 at Cl = 0.95, corresponding to 10.9 m/s.
For each forward foil considered separately, a span of 24 cm and area of 58 cm2results in an aspect ratio of
9.9. Because the previous planform area calculations assume an infinite wing, this area must be adjusted
for finite wingspans. Also, the upper surface of the foil at the struct junction has reduced lift generation. The
area is therefore increased to make up for these losses (Vellinga, 2009) to 80.6 cm2 and the span to 27 cm.
Aft
The main role of the aft foil is pitch stability, and it is sized to operate at a wing loading one half of the forward
foil. This reduced wing loading causes automatic pitch stability, as any pitching of the vessel would cause
relatively larger changes of Cl and therefore lift on the more lightly loaded aft foil. (Vellinga, 2009). That area
of 58 cm2results in a Cl/Cd of 30 (Cl = 0.25) at 15 m/s and a Cl/Cd of 22 (Cl = 0.14) at 20 m/s. Take-off speed
would be 6.85 m/s at a Cl/Cd of 68 (Cl = 1.2). Because this speed is lower than the take-off speed of the main
foil, the vessel would have sufficient pitch authority to avoid squatting during take-off.
The same aspect ratio adjustments were made to the aft foil. Because of the difficulty of constructing long
molds, both foils were considered to be span-limited and were given an elliptical planform with no washout
(Speer, n.d.).

Drive System

Jet pumps have been used many times in hydrofoil applications, most notably the Boeing 929 Jetfoil, PGH2, and Pegasus class (Williams, 1983). However, a jet pump small enough to fit the Lepidopteran would be
very difficult to source and would require a water pickup to be integrated into hydrofoil. A straight shaft Lepidopteran 8
inboard system would reduce transmission losses but would require a very long strut and accompanying
high drag loses while still producing a poor thrust angle. Therefore, an off-the-shelf gasoline outboard was
selected. The midsection and lower unit were mated to the electric motor, while the cowling, powerhead,
and controls were discarded. The driveshaft-mounted impeller was removed to reduce drag. Instead,
coolant water will be picked up from the same inlet and circulated by a 12v pump.
Transmission
The lower unit has a ratio of 2.42 to 1 and a maximum input speed of 6000 RPM, resulting in an output speed
of 2600 RPM. Because it is difficult to find the exact motor that has peak power at 6000 RPM, the motor was
mated to the driveshaft with a Gates HTD timing belt. This gives more flexibility with motor selection and
allows changes in RPM and torque during testing. Although the factory input speed limit is 6000 RPM, this is
only limited by bearing rating. If torque is kept below the gearset limits, the input shaft speed could
potentially be expanded past the factory limit with pulley ratio changes.
Motor
The motor was sized based on the power demands required by the propeller, and the rated power of the
donor outboard (10 hp, 7.4 kW). Two motors were considered: the 5 kW BLDC from GoldenMotor, and the
BadAss 6245-155Kv from Innov8tive Designs. While the 6245 had a rated continuous output of 4.7 kW and
more favorable motor velocity constant, we decided against it due to concerns about exceeding the duty
cycle of such a lightly constructed motor, as well as the difficulty of cooling and mounting an outrunner. A
number of no-name BLDC motors are available from outlets such as Amazon or Flipsky, but these products
were not even considered due to a lack of quality control and documentation.
Propeller
The factory propeller has three blades and measures 9.5 inches (24 cm) in diameter and 10 inches (25.4 cm)
in pitch. Assuming a slip of 5% and input shaft speed of 6000 RPM, this gives a maximum boat speed of only
9.4 m/s (18.2 kn). Aftermarket propellers are available with up to 12 inches of pitch. With the same
parameters, the maximum boat speed would be 11.8 m/s (23.0 kn). To meet the speed goal of 20 m/s, either
the existing propeller options must be spun twice as fast, or a higher pitch propeller must be designed. The
most common series, the Wageningen B-series, only covers P/D ratios up to 1.4. Other series, such as the
Gawn, KCA, and Newton-Rader, cover P/D ratios up to 2. The Newton-Rader series was selected because
they published both cavitation data and tabulated figures that were easier to work with. However, the Gawn
and KCA series offered similar performance. While a propeller with a diameter of 24 cm and a pitch of 50 cm
would reach the 20 m/s goal at a propeller shaft speed of 2500 RPM, it would do so with a power requirement
of over 20 kW. Thus, a compromise approach is necessary: The gearbox will run at a 50% overspeed to turn
a propeller 16 cm in diameter and 33.3 cm in pitch. At a full propeller RPM of 3750, the propeller will produce
341 N of thrust at an input power of 7.85 kW. This excess above the 5 kW motor rating is acceptable for short
duty cycle sprint speed goal of 20 kn. At a cruise speed of 15 m/s and propeller RPM of 3000, the propeller
will produce 286 N of thrust at an input power of 4.8 kW.
The Newton-Rader series assumes a hub to diameter ratio of 16.7%, while our lower unit geometry fixes hub
diameter at 6.6 cm. In lieu of a more advanced treatment, it was assumed that the thrust produced and
torque required would be reduced in proportion to the reduction in propulsor disk area. This 15% reduction
has already been accounted for in the calculations and figures. Wake fraction and thrust deduction were
both assumed to be zero, due to the high speed of the vessel and minimal hull interference. Lepidopteran 9
Figure 4 shows the amount of thrust produced as a function of vessel speed and propeller RPM, and figure
5 shows the same with the power required. The J values of 1.5 and 2.05 represent the lower and upper bound
of the 70% η efficiency band, while the 1.8 advance line is the peak operating point of 78% η efficiency.

CONSTRUCTION
Power Storage and Transmission
A Husky storage container is used as a waterproof container for the electronics. The battery and other
components are bolted to the box which is then bolted to the deck. The battery negative terminal is wired to
a Jiabaida JBD-AP21S002 battery management system. This BMS monitors cell voltage imbalances, state of
charge, charge and discharge current, and battery temperature. It automatically isolates the battery if
voltage is ever too high or too low and features a customizable software fuse, set to 200 A. The positive Lepidopteran 11
terminal of the battery has a 400 A fusible link connected to a 400A contactor energized by a disconnect
button accessible on top of the vessel. The 4 AWG wire used is rated for 160 A continuous duty3, well in
excess of the 150 A intermittent and 100 A continuous motor demands. The speed controller is a Golden
Motor EZkontrol B48800, rated for a working voltage of 48 V (max 75V) and bus current of 400 A.
Figure 7: Electronics Compartment View with Labels
A 52V 14S Intelligent Lithium Smart Charger from HPCBikes provides a slow but reliable and inexpensive
charging current of 3 A.
Gearcase and Mounting
A sheet of G10 FRP was laminated to the top aft surface of the board with 8 layers of 4oz unidirectional
carbon fiber. A custom pivot tube was fabricated from aluminum plate and tube to replace the bulky and
heavy factory outboard mounting system. The tiller arm was cut off, and the assembly bolted to the mounting
plate. The lower unit was disassembled, the gear surfaces and bearings were inspected for wear, and
reassembled. The motor mounting plate was fabricated out of ¼” aluminum plate, and a bearing pressed
into the plate to support the driveshaft.
A Gates HTD 5mm pitch timing belt with a 15mm width was selected. The 25mm width would’ve allowed
more margin of safety on the allowable torque transmitted, but the 25mm width had a much worse selection
of pulleys. Instead of aluminum, they were cast steel, and there were fewer different teeth counts available.
The two ratios selected were 1.94:1 and 3:1, which roughly corresponds4 with spinning the driveshaft at 6000
and 9000 RPM from a loaded motor RPM of 2900. Also, intermediate ratios of 2.25:1 and 2.58:1 could be
achieved by mixing pulleys between the two sets, in case optimum performance is somewhere in between.
Belt tension is achieved by rotating the motor in the housing, much like an automotive v-belt. Unfortunately,

Controls
Steering is controlled with a Savox SB-2290SG servo. It is rated for 70.0 kg-cm of
torque at 8.4 V. A bracket was fabricated and bolted to the outboard midsection
and a linkage connects to the servo arm.
The radio transmitter is a RadioMaster MT12 and the receiver is a RadioMaster
ER5C-i. They use the ELRS 2.4 GHz protocol, which offers superior flexibility for
programming and telemetry. A Speedybee F405 flight controller provides an
interface for telemetry data and (so far unutilized) autopilot functions. A Foxtech
HV BEC converts the main battery voltage to 8.4 V for the RC electronics and 12
V for the coolant pump.
The BLDC controller cannot interface directly with any of the RC electronics. The radio receiver outputs a 1
to 2 millisecond PWM signal, while the controller expects a 0-5v analog
input. Instead, the receiver drives a throttle servo which mechanically
actuates a potentiometer to provide the necessary analog signal.

TESTING AND EVALUATION
Due to many delays in fund processing, material delivery, and part fabrication, no on-the-water testing has
yet been done. However, everything is in order to perform testing and tuning over the next three weeks
leading into the competition. The questions that need to be answered are:
1. Which pulley ratios provide the best performance?
2. Which propeller provides the best performance?
3. What is the optimal CoG position?
4. Are motor, battery, and ESC cooling sufficient?
5. Is steering authority sufficient?
We can evaluate these conditions by running the vessel while changing one variable at a time. We can
directly monitor GPS speed, RPM, and component temperatures. By calculating slip from RPM and speed,
we can also find if the propeller is actually operating in an efficient regime. If battery cooling is insufficient,
a coolant plate can be added, and if the ESC and motor cooling is insufficient, the water pump could be
upgraded to a higher flow rate.
RISKS
There are three main weaknesses in our design:
1. The steering servo may have insufficient range or torque. The trade-off between torque and steering
range can be modified by lengthening or shortening the moment arm of either bracket. However,
while under load there will be much more force on the steering system than at rest, and it may prove
to be too much for the Savox servo. In that case, the servo can be replaced by a geared DC motor
with a reversible speed control that can output the torque required. However, since the race format
does not prioritize turning ability, it may be acceptable to just slow down for each turn.
2. Center of gravity may be too far aft. This can be determined by checking performance after relocating
the payload weight. If this is the case, the battery box could be moved further forward, which would
require new power cables; or the weight of the motor mounting plates and the outboard midsection
could be reduced by drilling lightening holes. Also, if there is extra buoyancy in the forward areas of
the hull, extra ballast could just be carried at the bow, or even extended in front of the bow on a sprit
structure. In the future, this imbalance could be mitigated by moving the motor forward of the pivot
point, but we chose the current location to simplify fabrication of the mounting plate and fitting of
the drive belt.
3. The gearbox may not be able to handle an input speed of 9000 RPM. We could not find any literature
discussing exactly why almost all outboard engines are limited to 6000 RPM, but hypothesize that is
only because of limitation in the combustion powerhead. The gear sets are typically limited by
torque, not RPM, and bearings of the size used in the lower unit usually have speed limits well over
10,000 RPM. Since this 50% was the only practical way to hit our speed targets, we considered this
an acceptable risk, especially considering the short duration of the race. By intentionally running the
lower unit under more demanding conditions during testing than during the race, by performing Lepidopteran 14
frequent oil changes, and by examining the gears and bearings for abnormal wear, we will find out if
running at the elevated speed is acceptable. If not, we will simply run the race at reduced speed.
FUTURE DEVELOPMENT
Lepidopteran is ripe for ongoing modification and use. The manageable size, high speed, good endurance,
and payload capacity mean it could be used for other marine projects as well as future PEP competitions.
The following are some of the avenues that we think may be worth pursuing:
1. Hydrofoils
a. The foil section, planform, or lift distribution could be improved. Particularly of interest may
be changing the elliptical planform to a bell-shaped lift distribution, which would be more
efficient with respect to strength.
b. The foil manufacturing process could be improved. Perhaps they could be milled out of billet
stainless steel (some of the latest Moth hydrofoils have done this), or just laid up with an
improved method, like VARTM.
c. The subcavitating foils could be changed to supercavitating. They would be more inefficient
but offer the possibility to break the 50 kn barrier.
d. The entire foil system could be switched to a surface piercing configuration.
2. Gearbox – the current lower unit gearbox is probably the single biggest area for improvement. The
outboard that we chose uses a through hub exhaust, which is bulky and increases drag of the lower
unit, while providing zero utility to an electric system. Also, the very low gear ratio of 2.42 to 1 is more
suited for a sailboat or a dinghy than a performance high speed vessel. Both of these aspects could
be improved by selecting a lower unit similar to those used by racing boats.
